extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in hoaxes, media watchers, and those studying photojournalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Documenting and evaluating a doctored news photograph (the LA Times/Brian Walski Basra composite) to illustrate standards and failures in photojournalism authenticity and editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: No undisclosed composites or manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The photo was actually a composite of two other photos (middle and bottom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs published as news should not be composites or otherwise altered without disclosure. The Walski case shows that creating a composite and publishing it as a single authentic scene breaches journalistic standards (the LA Times fired him).

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for duplicated elements as evidence of manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A staffer at the Courant noticed that some figures in the image appeared to have been duplicated. For instance, the back of a person squatting down ... was identical to the back of the person directly to the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and fact-checkers should visually inspect images for repeating patterns or identical figures (duplication) as a red flag indicating digital compositing or cloning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial query and verification procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The staffer queried the Times's Director of Photography about this, who then contacted Walski. Walski admitted the photo was actually a composite of two other photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should have procedures to query photographers when anomalies are spotted and to require explanations or original source frames; prompt inquiry can confirm authenticity and trigger corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and admission of alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Walski admitted the photo was actually a composite of two other photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When manipulation is detected, the photographer and outlet should be transparent about what was done; admission enables correction, explanation, and appropriate editorial response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for ethical breaches
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant editorial sanctions (retraction, firing, public editor's note) are an expected outcome when a news organization publishes deceptive images, underscoring accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of how easily images can be manipulated
rubrics_metrics.description: The scandal ... underscored how easy the manipulation of images had become -- so easy that a convincing composite could be created in a few minutes by a photographer working in a war zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the low technical barrier to creating convincing composites, news organizations, fact-checkers, and the public must remain vigilant; quick digital manipulation does not excuse failure to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer intent and ethical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Walski: 'There was no reason to do [what I did]. I was playing around a little bit. I said, "that looks good." I worked it and sent it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing intent (carelessness, experimentation, or deliberate deception) is part of evaluating misconduct; even 'playing around' that results in deceptive images violates professional ethics.
